languages: 77 languages (translated from 99), including high-resource and low-resource languages

links.outcome: Ambient scribe transcription quality and serious clinical risk by language resource level
links.effect: Low-resource languages had worse WER than high-resource (β=+0.078, 95% CI +0.045 to +0.111; p<0.0001) but no detectable difference in CRITICAL/HIGH risk (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.43; p=0.72).
links.quote: At complexity level 3, low-resource languages had worse WER than high-resource languages (β=+0.078, 95% CI +0.045 to +0.111; p<0.0001), without a detectable difference in CRITICAL/HIGH risk (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.43; p=0.72).

links.outcome: Whether frequency metrics like WER track clinically consequential scribe transcription errors
links.effect: None of six frequency metrics showed detectable association with serious clinical risk (|Spearman ρ|<0.16); 251 (0.42%) of 59,819 errors CRITICAL/HIGH; clinical-risk assessment complements WER.
links.quote: None of six frequency metrics showed a statistically detectable association with serious clinical risk across languages; correlations were small (absolute Spearman ρ<0.16).

unlisted_practices: Using severity-by-likelihood clinical-risk rating (LLM-as-rater) of scribe errors instead of WER alone for evaluation

screen.reason: The study benchmarks ambient scribes across 77 languages and specifically evaluates a deployment validation practice: using a clinical safety risk framework (Severity x Likelihood) versus standard WER metrics to safeguard against consequential transcription errors.

primary.practice: clinical risk evaluation framework for ambient scribes
